title: A large-scale comparison of human-written versus ChatGPT-generated essays
extended_summary:
This paper examines how well generative AI—specifically ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4—can produce argumentative essays compared with human-written student essays. The central question is whether AI-generated essays match or exceed the quality of essays associated with secondary-school writing tasks, and how the language characteristics of AI-generated essays differ from student writing. The study is motivated by concerns that generative AI may substantially disrupt writing instruction and homework assessment.

The authors used 90 argumentative essay prompts drawn from an online essay forum frequented by German high-school students. For each topic, they compared one existing human-written essay with new essays generated by ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 using a simple zero-shot prompt. A total of 111 secondary-school teachers participated as raters after attending a two-hour online training session about ChatGPT; 658 ratings were collected across 270 essays. Teachers scored essays blind to source on seven rubric dimensions related to content and language quality, and the authors also conducted computational linguistic analyses of lexical diversity, syntactic complexity, nominalization, modality, epistemic markers, and discourse markers.

The study context is secondary education, but it is not an instructional intervention study and does not test AI feedback on student writing. Rather, it compares essay products written by students versus essays generated directly by AI. The student essays were written by non-native English-speaking high-school-aged users of an online essay forum, and the raters were secondary-school teachers in Germany. The essays appear to correspond mainly to grades 11-13; for the requested taxonomy this maps most closely to high school.

The main conclusion is that both ChatGPT versions produced argumentative essays rated significantly higher than the human-written student essays across all assessed criteria, with ChatGPT-4 generally outperforming ChatGPT-3.5. The authors also found systematic linguistic differences between human and AI writing styles. They argue that educators should adapt writing instruction and assessment practices in response to the availability of generative AI. However, the paper does not provide a direct comparator study of AI writing feedback versus teacher, peer, or other feedback conditions in secondary-school writing instruction.
quality_tier_rationale: Peer-reviewed, large-scale comparative rating study with clear methods and statistical testing, but it is not an intervention trial and lacks random assignment of students to feedback conditions. It is best classified as observational/comparative evidence rather than causal evidence of an educational intervention effect.
impact_tier_rationale: The observed differences in essay-quality ratings between human and AI-generated essays are consistently medium to very large (many effects > 0.20, several > 0.80). However, this impact reflects comparative output quality of AI-generated text, not student learning gains from a classroom writing-feedback intervention.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 used to generate argumentative high-school-style essays for direct comparison against human-written student essays rated by secondary-school teachers.

finding.finding_summary: This study directly assessed writing quality of argumentative essays, comparing human-written student essays with ChatGPT-3 and ChatGPT-4 outputs across 90 prompts. Across seven rubric dimensions, AI-generated essays were rated significantly higher than human-written essays by secondary-school teachers; overall mean scores were 3.69 for humans, 4.36 for ChatGPT-3, and 4.68 for ChatGPT-4, with human vs. ChatGPT-3 effect sizes ranging from d=0.52 to 1.15 and human vs. ChatGPT-4 from d=0.88 to 1.43. The paper is not a feedback-intervention comparator study; it evaluates generated essay quality rather than student revision after feedback.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of argumentative essay quality on seven rubric criteria: topic/completeness, logic/composition, expressiveness/comprehensiveness, language mastery, complexity, vocabulary/text linking, and language constructs
finding.study_size: 90 topics; 270 essays total (90 human, 90 ChatGPT-3, 90 ChatGPT-4); 658 ratings from 111 teachers
finding.effect_size: Human vs ChatGPT-3: d=0.52 to 1.15 across criteria; Human vs ChatGPT-4: d=0.88 to 1.43; ChatGPT-3 vs ChatGPT-4 significant on some criteria with d=0.45 to 0.50
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI for mean ratings reported via bootstrap, exact intervals not_reported in provided text
finding.std_deviation: Overall SDs: human=1.26, ChatGPT-3=1.14, ChatGPT-4=1.11; criterion-level SDs reported, e.g., language mastery human=1.37, ChatGPT-3=1.19, ChatGPT-4=1.08
